Q: How to implement idempotency across multiple servers with non-shared databases and private caches? A:

I think we might need to structure things a bit that seem to be mixed in the question. There are the concerns of:

  1. Idempotency
  2. Deduplication
  3. Locality

Idempotency means the result of performing the operation multiple times on the same arguments has the same outcome as performing it once, iirc. So your creation operation may well be naturally idempotent. If your goal is to have an idempotent create operation, you can implement it so that creating an account with an ID that already exists is a no-op.

Deduplication seems to be more what you are talking about. To deduplicate across multiple instances based on a key, these instances need to have access to the same data, i.e. your store of known keys. So that won't work in the setup you describe. But I don't think that matters, because what also doesn't work in that setup is

Locality. Not sure if that's the right term, but in your setup, how do you know which account lies on which server? What if you want to read the account data, or perform subsequent operations on the account? How would you know if you need to go to server A or B?

So the options are:

  • Both servers use the same cache. If your servers are instances of the same application, in the same region, that would be a common approach. Or
  • If your servers are instances of the same application, but can't share the cache for some reason, you'll need to partition your data, and route requests either to service A or B, based on the accountID. Or
  • If your servers are actually different applications, you should decide which one's responsible for account creation.

To your questions:

  1. Yes, but not by deduplication, only if your commands are naturally idempotent. For deduplication, each service needs to see the known keys.
  2. See text above - for deduplication, either yes or partition your data.
  3. I'd say if you want to keep the caches separate, sharding / horizontal partitioning would be the name of the pattern.
  4. Certainly not required. Also that poses the question why you have the two separate caches.

Speaking of which, why do you have the two separate caches? What's the relationship between service A and service B? You'll get better answers if you give more context.

Q: Assign Normal Distribution Function to an Array A:

My following answer is based on the assumption that the variables name you used really mean something (Range Average, Range Standard Deviation). In such a case, VBA is able to return an array if you transform the range in an array (inside the function).

In such circumstances, your function needs to be looking as:


Function NormDistr(r As Range, average As Double, std As Double) As Variant

 NormDistr = Application.Norm_Dist(r.value, average, std, False)
             'it works only replacing WorksheetFunctionn with Application...

End Function

And it can be called in the next way (I used a specific range, you need to use yours):

Sub NormDistrArray()
  Dim arrND, r As Range
  Set r = Range("H2:H13") 'use here your necessary range
  arrND = NormDistr(r, WorksheetFunction.average(r), WorksheetFunction.StDev(r))

  Debug.Print UBound(arrND) 'it returns the array number of elements
  Debug.Print Join(Application.Transpose(arrND), vbCrLf) 'it returns the array elements separated by VbCrLf
End Sub

In order to see the return in Immediate Window, you need to press `Ctrl + G`, being in VBE (Visual Basic Editor)

Q: How can I using yield list element infinitely A:

The following solution without dependencies is an improved revisitation of previous solutions:

def gen(lst):
    while True:
        yield from lst

Usage:

>>> g = gen(['a','b','c'])

>>> for x in g:
>>>     do something...
>>>     if some_reason:
>>>         break

>>> [next(g) for _ in range(7)]
['a', 'b', 'c', 'a', 'b', 'c', 'a']

Alternatively, if you want a limit to the cycling generator, you can use the following version which allows you to set (optionally) the total length of the output sequence:

def gen(lst,limit=None):
    if type(limit) == int:
        g = gen(lst)
        for _ in range(limit):
            yield next(g)
        return
    yield from lst
    yield from gen(lst,limit)

Usage:

>>> g = gen(['a','b','c'], limit=7))

>>> for x in g:
>>>     do something (for 7 times)...

>>> list(g)
['a', 'b', 'c', 'a', 'b', 'c', 'a']

N.B. If the limit you set is greater than Python recursion capabilities (usually 1000 recursions) you can improve such capabilities through the following code:

>>> import sys
>>> sys.setrecursionlimit(some_greater_limit)

Q: What is the dependency inversion principle and why is it important? A:

Another interpretation: just forget the Dependency inversion and call it Use driven development instead.

Let's say you have DB, Calc and Stats modules. Calc and Stats fetch DB data and save it back to DB. DB in traditional clean modular design is not supposed to be aware about other two modules.

Traditional (non DI):
DB interface have "Turing complete" goal on itself, i.e. to cover most of the expected current and future use cases with standard set of methods. Development iteration may start with DB and interface update and expected next step is consequent Calc and Stats refactoring or synchronisation or rebuild.

  • other modules include and call DB methods and thus must be aware of DB interface design
  • DB is not aware how exactly it's used
  • all 3 modules can be drivers of the system evolution

Use driven development (DI):
Calc and Stats additionally declare and self-contain the way they expect to interact with something that represents DB. These interfaces in Calc and Stats are updated first to match new development iteration. And as side effect of these new requests, DB must be updated because it directly includes interfaces from Calc and Stats. Goal of DB is narrowed down to support a set of known interfaces.

  • Calc and Stats declare what they need, but do not reference specific DB module
  • DB explicitly includes use cases from other modules in form of interfaces
  • DB is clearly not the driver of the system evolution

So it starts to be simple if to replace S0LID with SOLIU.
But as soon as such decoupling from DB is considered, extracting communication methods (interfaces) from Stats and Calc to the separate declaration (lowest level) could be the better solution: it emphasises that communication interface is negotiated by all actors rather than enforced from one side (from DB or from use cases).

Q: Why is passing a column name as a parameter in PyMySQL not working A:

PyMySQL is treating trigger_column as a string value, not as a column identifier. So if trigger_column = "email_alert", the query becomes:


SELECT alert_name FROM alerts WHERE org_id = 123 AND 'email_alert' = 1

it compares the literal string 'email_alert' to 1, which is always false, hence no results

you need to handle the column names differently:

# define allowed column names
ALLOWED_TRIGGER_COLUMNS = {'email_alert', 'sms_alert', 'slack_alert', 'webhook_alert'}

if trigger_column not in ALLOWED_TRIGGER_COLUMNS:
    raise ValueError(f"Invalid trigger column: {trigger_column}")

# now its safe to use in query
query = f"SELECT alert_name FROM alerts WHERE org_id = %s AND {trigger_column} = 1"
cursor.execute(query, (org_id,))

Safest way to do it since you explicitly control which column names are allowed.

However, if you need more flexibility but still want to be safe, use backticks to quote the identifier and validate it doesn't contain backticks:

def quote_identifier(identifier):
    if '`' in identifier:
        raise ValueError("Identifier cannot contain backticks")
    return f"`{identifier}`"

# Using it
safe_column = quote_identifier(trigger_column)
query = f"SELECT alert_name FROM alerts WHERE org_id = %s AND {safe_column} = 1"
cursor.execute(query, (org_id,))
